plan.topic: Tirzepatide vs semaglutide 7.2 mg ('Wegovy HD'): 4.5 percentage points more average weight loss for tirzepatide's highest dose in a Lilly-sponsored indirect comparison of SURMOUNT-1 and STEP UP (adults with obesity, EASD 2026)
plan.angle: 'Tirzepatide vs semaglutide 7.2 mg: what an indirect comparison can and can't tell you.' Slides: (1) the question; (2) what an ITC is: two separate trials, statistically adjusted, not randomized against each other; (3) 4.5 points (highest dose) and 3.2 points (middle dose) more average weight loss for tirzepatide, with the qualifier 'indirect · Lilly-funded · adults with obesity without T2D · 72 weeks · treatment-regimen estimand · conference data'. Add on the same slide: 'On-treatment analysis: difference not statistically significant.' (4) each trial's raw average, labelled as separate trials; (5) the one true head-to-head, SURMOUNT-5, vs semaglutide 2.4 mg, with its population and timeframe, instead of the unverified Int J Obes item; (6) what matters for you: health conditions, tolerability, coverage and access; (7) questions for your prescriber. No verdict and no switching advice. Title: 'Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide 7.2 mg: 4.5 Points More Weight Loss in a Lilly-Funded Indirect Comparison, Not Head-to-Head'.

plan.why: 'Zepbound vs Wegovy' is a perennial high-volume search with a fresh EASD hook. Consumer explainers haven't caught up, and the honest 'not head-to-head' correction is our contrarian-but-true piece. | fact-check: The core figures check out: Lilly release (PR Newswire, 29 Sep 2026) and EASD 2026 abstract. The indirect treatment comparison used SURMOUNT-1 data (a subgroup, per the abstract) and STEP UP, in adults with obesity (BMI ≥30) without type 2 diabetes, at 72 weeks. Mean differences were −4.5 points for tirzepatide 15 mg and −3.2 points for 10 mg (treatment-regimen estimand). The analysis was Lilly-funded. Raw averages: 20.2% in SURMOUNT-1 (15 mg) and 13.7% in STEP UP (7.2 mg). Two things the angle leaves out would change how viewers read it. (1) Using the efficacy estimand (on-treatment), the difference was NOT statistically significant (1.8 points for 15 mg). That has to go on the result slide. (2) A real head-to-head trial exists, SURMOUNT-5 (tirzepatide vs semaglutide 2.4 mg, NEJM 2025). 'Which works best? This isn't head-to-head' must say there's no head-to-head against 7.2 mg, not that no head-to-head exists at all. I couldn't find the 'independent Int J Obes indirect comparison (28 Sep)'. Search only turned up Int J Obes ITCs in type 2 diabetes (SURMOUNT-2 vs STEP 2). Drop slide 5 unless the writer confirms the exact paper, date, population and that it compares against 7.2 mg. The 20.2% SURMOUNT-1 figure may be for the full trial rather than the subgroup used in the ITC, so label it as such. Avoid the 'Wegovy HD' brand as a lead. Verified sources: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lillys-zepbound-tirzepatide-10-mg-and-15-mg-was-associated-with-more-weight-loss-than-wegovy-hd-semaglutide-injection-7-2-mg-in-a-new-indirect-treatment-comparison-302892601.html ; https://endo2026.endocrine.org/ajaxcalls/PresentationInfo.asp?PresentationID=1845277

social.instagram_caption:
Tirzepatide vs semaglutide 7.2 mg — who's actually ahead? 🤔

Spoiler: we found no head-to-head trial of tirzepatide vs the 7.2 mg dose (as of Sept 2026).

Here's what a new Lilly-funded EASD 2026 analysis actually did and found:
→ Took two separate trials (SURMOUNT-1 for tirzepatide, STEP UP for semaglutide 7.2 mg) and statistically adjusted for differences between the groups
→ In adults with obesity, no type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks: tirzepatide 15 mg showed ~4.5 percentage points more average weight loss than semaglutide 7.2 mg
→ But look at on-treatment results only, and that gap wasn't statistically significant
→ A real randomized trial does exist (SURMOUNT-5) — but it compared tirzepatide to semaglutide 1.7/2.4 mg, not the 7.2 mg "HD" dose. We found no head-to-head trial against 7.2 mg (as of Sept 2026)

An indirect comparison is an estimate, not a race. And it's funded by the company that makes tirzepatide, which matters when you read the headline.

Tirzepatide or semaglutide 7.2 mg — which one wins on weight loss? A new Lilly-funded analysis presented at EASD 2026 tried to answer that by statistically comparing two separate trials (SURMOUNT-1 and STEP UP), not a real head-to-head race.

In adults with obesity and no type 2 diabetes, the 15 mg tirzepatide dose was linked to about 4.5 percentage points more average weight loss than semaglutide 7.2 mg over 72 weeks. But when researchers looked only at people who stayed on treatment, the difference wasn't statistically significant. There IS a real randomized head-to-head trial (SURMOUNT-5), but it compared tirzepatide to semaglutide 1.7/2.4 mg, not the 7.2 mg dose — so we found no direct head-to-head trial against the 7.2 mg dose (as of Sept 2026).

Averages don't predict your individual result, and this analysis was funded by the maker of tirzepatide. Full breakdown (with sources) is in our carousel. What questions would you ask your doctor about choosing between these?

factcheck.summary: Every number and study description matches its source. S1: Lilly's release from 29 Sep 2026 on the EASD 2026 presentation. It gives 4.5 points (15 mg) and 3.2 points (10 mg) using the treatment-regimen estimand, and 1.8 and 0.7 points on-treatment, both not statistically significant. The work was Lilly-funded, compared adults with obesity and no T2D at 72 weeks, and was adjusted for sex, age, baseline weight and A1C. It also says there is no head-to-head trial against 7.2 mg. S2: search results confirm the ENDO 2026 abstract (Wilding and Postma, 13 June 2026). It used a SURMOUNT-1 subgroup with BMI ≥30 and no T2D, compared with the whole STEP UP population at week 72. SURMOUNT-1: −20.9% vs −3.1% on placebo. STEP UP: −18.7% vs −3.9% on placebo. SURMOUNT-5: 751 adults, open-label, highest tolerated dose, −20.2% vs −13.7%, waist −18.4 vs −13.0 cm. The framing is careful throughout. It says "indirect, not head-to-head", flags the Lilly funding, reports the on-treatment results that weren't significant, warns against subtracting across trials, hedges the date on "no head-to-head vs 7.2 mg", mentions GI side effects and includes the prescriber line. No dosing advice and no gray-market sources. There are only minor fixes: define the subgroup, add the comorbidity qualifier for overweight in SURMOUNT-1, add the uncertainty range, and add a hint in the title that on-treatment wasn't significant.

issues.problem: The subgroup isn't defined, so viewers can't tell why it differs from the full SURMOUNT-1 results on slide 4. The adjustment variables aren't named either.
issues.fix: Two separate trials, statistically adjusted (sex, age, baseline weight, A1C), never randomized against each other. It used only SURMOUNT-1 participants with BMI 30+ and no type 2 diabetes. Source: EASD 2026 presentation (Lilly release, 29 Sep 2026); ENDO 2026 abstract.

issues.problem: SURMOUNT-1 only enrolled people with overweight (BMI 27+) if they also had at least one weight-related condition. Without that qualifier the population sounds broader than it was.
issues.fix: Obesity, or overweight + a weight-related condition; no diabetes

issues.problem: It's a model estimate with a wide uncertainty range (95% CrI 2.8–6.3 points), but it's shown as a single number.
issues.fix: Change the detail to: 'Treatment-regimen estimand · range 2.8–6.3 pts'. For 10 mg: 'Treatment-regimen estimand · range 1.4–5.0 pts'.
